result:
At the back of the train station, between a vending machine and a door marked STAFF ONLY, there was a shelf for things people had forgotten.

Most of it was ordinary: gloves without partners, water bottles, an umbrella that had turned inside out and stayed that way. Then one afternoon, someone left a small clay bird. It was lopsided, painted blue, and too heavy to fly even in the imagination.

The station attendant set it on the highest shelf, where it could watch the platforms. For weeks nobody claimed it. Commuters began to notice it while waiting for delayed trains. A child waved to it every Tuesday. Someone tucked a paper scarf around its neck in December.

In spring, a woman came in and described the bird exactly. She had made it with her father years ago and lost it on the day she moved out of the city. The attendant fetched it down. Before handing it over, he told her about the scarf and the Tuesday waves.

She held the bird in both hands for a moment. “It had a good time here,” she said.

Outside, a train arrived.
